title: In the Modern Era of Distraction Addiction, You Need This Skill
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston argues that sustained attention is becoming one of the scarcest and most valuable professional skills, and that the hyper-connected smartphone era is eroding it. He describes his own former days of constant email, buzzing phones and fragmented meetings, and says the worst cost was that it made listening to his wife and others harder. Drawing on Cal Newport's Deep Work, he covers the myth of multitasking and attentional residue, and the claim that workplaces built on open offices and instant messaging reward distraction. He proposes that impact equals time spent multiplied by quality of focus, and offers practical steps: admit the problem, identify your deep work, schedule protected blocks, remove distractions and schedule recovery. He closes with a leadership application: build team policies, such as batching meetings and making many optional, that protect deep work for everyone.
points: Impact in almost any field is time spent multiplied by quality of focus, so fragmenting attention quietly caps the value of the hours worked.
Attentional residue means part of your mind stays on the last email or meeting, which makes the next task worse even when you appear to switch cleanly.
The author's own cost of constant connectivity was relational as well as professional, because distraction made it harder to listen to his wife and colleagues.
Deep work is a trainable skill that begins with scheduled, protected blocks of about an hour, with phones out of reach and email off.
Leaders should change organizational norms, for example by batching meetings and making many optional, rather than leaving deep work to individual willpower.
quotes: Research from neuroscience and performance psychology is beginning to paint a compelling picture: people in the modern world may be damaging their ability to sustain attention, concentration, and focus.
Every new message was like a torpedo to my concentration, often sending me down numerous rabbit holes.

He includes a wealth of compelling research, from the myths of multitasking to attentional residue—what happens when we move from one task to the next, but a portion of our attention remains stuck on our last meeting or email, preventing us from fully concentrating on the new task.
We have traded deep work for the ability to get ahold of each other immediately.
Think about it this way: your overall impact in almost anything will be the result of time spent multiplied by quality of focus.
We have inadvertently trained our brains to prefer the pleasure hit of rapid, shallow tasks, but we can work to reverse this tendency.
Start with one hour several days per week of completely uninterrupted time. Schedule these blocks into your week in advance to do your deep work. Protect them at all costs.
if you are in a position of leadership for your organization, make sure that you set up organizational practices and policies that foster deep work for your team.
